items.name: Renewable Energy Technologies -- CONTROL r0
items.response:
Adjudication between competing accounts of a system black rests on reconstructing a single, time-stamped sequence of events rather than on prior views about generation technology. Operators and investigators align fault-recorder traces, protection logs and interconnector flow measurements on a common clock, so that every candidate explanation must be made consistent with one and the same record. That tornadoes toppled transmission towers on two 275 kV lines north of Adelaide shows that a severe storm on 28 September 2016 damaged transmission infrastructure in South Australia. The towers collapsed because of corrosion of their foundations; that explanation cannot be squared with the toppling of the towers by tornadoes on the lines north of Adelaide, for both cannot hold of the same structures.

The tower failures produced a sequence of voltage dips across the South Australian network, and those dips caused the wind turbines' voltage ride-through protection to activate once a preset number of dips had been exceeded. Because that ride-through protection activated, nine wind farms sustained a reduction in power output following the voltage disturbances. The abrupt fall in wind generation caused import flow on the Heywood Interconnector to rise steeply, and that surge in flow in turn caused the interconnector to trip on loss of synchronism. The interconnector trip resulted in approximately 850,000 customers losing electricity supply.

The restoration record is the next point of contention, and it admits of only two possibilities: either supply was restored to all customers within eight hours of the blackout, or some customers remained without supply more than eight hours after it. One of the two must be the case, and they cannot both be.

Attribution of responsibility then turns on two deficiencies, at least one of which obtained and perhaps both: that the wind farms' voltage ride-through protection settings were set too conservatively for the local network conditions, or that the transmission network's fault level was inadequate to support the connected inverter-based generation. Whereas the protection settings are faulted as unduly conservative for the network in which they sat, the market operator concluded that the storm damage alone would have blacked out South Australia regardless of the wind farms' response.

What ultimately settles the apportionment is documentary and metrological rather than rhetorical: the as-commissioned protection-setting registers retrieved from each turbine controller, the turbine-level dip counters, and the measured fault levels at each connection point, read against the tower failure records and the interconnector's flow and angle traces. Where those records show protection operating exactly as configured, the configuration itself, and the network strength it was configured for, becomes the object of the finding, and responsibility is divided according to which of the two could have been altered under the connection rules then in force.

claims.text: A severe storm on 28 September 2016 damaged transmission infrastructure in South Australia.
Tornadoes toppled transmission towers on two 275 kV lines north of Adelaide.
The tower failures produced a sequence of voltage dips across the South Australian network.
Nine wind farms sustained a reduction in power output following the voltage disturbances.
The wind turbines' voltage ride-through protection activated after a preset number of voltage dips was exceeded.
The abrupt fall in wind generation increased import flow on the Heywood Interconnector.
The Heywood Interconnector tripped on loss of synchronism.
The Australian Energy Market Operator published a final incident report into the event.
High-speed fault recorder and SCADA data were used to reconstruct the sequence of events.
The wind farm operators had not disclosed the ride-through protection settings to the market operator before the event.
The Australian Energy Regulator commenced Federal Court proceedings against four wind farm operators.
Software changes to the turbine control systems removed the ride-through limitation after the event.
Approximately 850,000 customers lost electricity supply during the event.
The market operator required wind farms to resubmit model data and protection settings after the event.
The market operator concluded that the storm damage alone would have blacked out South Australia regardless of the wind farms' response.
The transmission towers collapsed due to corrosion of their foundations.
The Federal Court dismissed all allegations against the wind farm operators.
The blackout was initiated by a trip of the Torrens Island gas-fired power station.
Supply was restored to all customers within eight hours of the blackout.
Some customers remained without supply more than eight hours after the blackout.
The wind farms' voltage ride-through protection settings were set too conservatively for the local network conditions.
The transmission network's fault level was inadequate to support the connected inverter-based generation.
The loss of 456 MW of wind generation preceded the interconnector trip.
The interconnector tripped after 456 MW of wind output had already been lost.
The Federal Court found that four wind farm operators breached their generator performance standards.
The final incident report concluded that the sustained reduction in wind farm output was the critical factor leading to the interconnector trip.
